title: The Sandwich Approach That's Reshaping Classroom AI: Washington State's Case for Starting and Ending with Humans
author: Andrew Marcinek
summary: Marcinek examines Washington State's 2024 human-centered AI guidance for K-12 schools, built on a Human, AI, Human framework in which every AI interaction starts with human inquiry and ends with human reflection. He reads the framework as a philosophy of learning disguised as a workflow, one that also supports student wellbeing by slowing students down before they prompt and keeping their own voice after the output arrives. He contrasts the state's empowerment framing with fear-based guidance that produces secret use and unread policies, and credits its deliberately evolving, iterated design. Examples include an advisory group with a student member, an educator innovator cohort, and a tiny rural school using AI for accessibility while guarding student data. The piece closes with a Monday classroom routine: students write the question, what they already know and how they will judge the answer before using the tool, then say what the AI missed.
points: The Human, AI, Human sandwich puts the thinking before and after the tool, so AI becomes a collaborator in a process the student has already set in motion.
Beginning with inquiry and ending with reflection is both good AI practice and a metacognitive wellbeing practice.
Student misuse of AI is framed as a thinking problem, not a technology problem, which guidance should address directly.
Fear-based AI policies tend to produce fear-based cultures, with teachers avoiding tools and students using them in secret.
Treating state guidance as a living, iterated document builds culture rather than compliance.
quotes: The concept is disarmingly simple: every interaction with AI should begin with a human and end with a human.
When we ask a student to begin with inquiry, we’re asking them to slow down. To think before they prompt. To know what they’re looking for before they go looking.

The alternative—the one many of us worry about—is a student who opens an AI tool with no question in mind, accepts the first output as truth, and submits it without a second thought. That’s not a technology problem. That’s a thinking problem.

A lot of AI guidance documents are built on fear—fear of cheating, fear of data breaches, fear of losing control. And those concerns are real. But fear-based frameworks tend to produce fear-based cultures.

It assumes that AI is already here. That students and educators are already using it. And that the job of the state isn’t to police that usage, but to shape it—to build the habits of mind that make AI use thoughtful rather than thoughtless.
That posture—of humility, of iteration—is itself a form of digital wellness. It says: we don’t have all the answers yet, and that’s okay.
